newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION- S.AFRICA ON DARK SIDE OF MOON - BY T.TWINE.
newsitem.headline: OPINION- S.AFRICA ON DARK SIDE OF MOON - BY T.TWINE.

text.p: By Tony Twine, an economist at Econometrix financial consultancy

We South Africans are a crazy bunch of mankind, for several reasons. For example, take the case of yours truly and wife boarding an aircraft at late one afternoon in mid-December at a balmy 26 degrees centigrade, only to emerge from the aircraft in London at seven the next morning at a frosty minus three degrees.
Little did we suspect that was only the beginning - the big freeze of New Year 1997 was still a fortnight in the future.
But, in case you may think that we were going to spend the yuletide season longing for the warmth of home, we were not, for a couple of very good reasons.

Firstly, even though the snow stayed mainly in the air, wherever we went the cities, towns and villages were all decked out with the trappings of Christmas to an extent and an effect which can never be replicated in the heat and dust of South Africa.

But the second reason was not made of all that yo-ho-ho stuff, and left a small chill on the spirit which refuses to thaw out, even after a week of being back in harness in the southern hemisphere summer.
One is allowed to forget about South Africa and its warmth of a million yule logs simply because, as you emerge from terminal whatever at Heathrow, South Africa simply ceases to exist.
The sun may have been beating down back home, but, as far as media exposure is concerned, it is out in the cold.

Perhaps our exposure to the media was a little biased in as much it was focused on radio and television, with less emphasis on the press, but even the few newspapers which came our way were virtually devoid of any meaningful news - the opening of the old prison on Robben Island is quaint, rather than meaningful, but there it was.

Apart from the newspaper article about the island, one of its previous inhabitants got some glowing coverage in the Queen's Christmas day message - Nelson Mandela clearly has touched the heart of the 70 year old monarch, but probably not because he has been divorced once more often than is par in the British Royal family.

Through contacts with foreign correspondents visiting or resident in South Africa, one has been made aware of how South Africa's flavour-of-the-month status disintegrated in the foreign media after the inauguration of the Mandela government in May 1994. No blood equals no news.
Back home, however, it probably does not sink in in quite the literal sense in which it exists in reality.

Traditional British Europhobia currently draws their attention towards the Eastern horizon as round two of the Battle of Britain takes place at Westminster. Hong Kong is a hot foreign news item, understandably so because of its special circumstances in 1997.

Interestingly, Australia is here, there and everywhere in the British media, even though the Brits and the Aussies do not seem to hold each other in particularly high regard. The Australians have marketed themselves well, even if it has been done mainly through hour after never-ending hour of soap operas and Rolf Harris being kind to animals even dumber than himself. Who cares how they have achieved it - alongside Hong Kong this winter, they are certainly streets ahead of any other region of British ex-influence.

Of course media exposure on an all-pervasive level is of tremendous importance when trying to promote trade, investment, tourism, support for economic development policies and foreign relations initiatives. Most of the British do not even know how to pronounce Trevor Manuel's name the way that he does - how can they, or anyone else making investment decisions, be expected to believe in him, his government, its policies or the country which it represents.

If that was the impression of isolation picked up in London, what must coverage of South Africa be like in investment capitals around the world with much less direct involvement and interest than the UK?
South Africa has marketed itself badly, if at all, over the past three years, and the turkeys, for want of a seasonal phrase, are coming home to roost.

When the only decent coverage you get in a few weeks is a nostalgic mention of your president in the Queen's Christmas speech, the writing is as on the wall for your currency as it is for your aspirations.
Remembering that bad news always travels fastest and furthest, when there is bad news about South Africa it stands out starkly.

South Africa is in desperate need of a concerted marketing campaign, not for a few weeks or a few months, but for decades to come. Without it, more astronauts will have seen the dark side of the moon than there will be investors who know anything about this country.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
